newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina to hold three-way labor talks next week.
newsitem.headline: Argentina to hold three-way labor talks next week.

text.p: Argentine trade unions and business leaders said Friday they will meet with the government early next week to define where they agree and disagree on proposed labor law reforms to be sent to Congress.

The Group of Eight business chambers and CGT main labor federation, at loggerheads over how to reduce unemployment, were still finalizing details for talks with Cabinet Chief Jorge Rodriguez and Labor Minister Armando Caro Figueroa.
"But there will be a meeting Monday or Tuesday, with all three sides, probably in the Casa Rosada (government house)," one senior CGT source told Reuters.
"In principle that's the way it is," Jorge Di Fiori, head of the Chamber of Commerce and a Group of Eight heavyweight, told reporters. "It could produce some sort of definition."
The CGT source said there were also plans for closed-door talks with the Group of Eight later Friday "to see if we can reach consensus on 60 or 70 percent of the agenda."
In a further sign a breakthrough could come after a tough week's negotiations, the embattled Caro Figueroa said: "An agreement with both sides is now much closer than a week ago."
The Peronist government desperately needs good news on the 17.3 percent unemployment rate ahead of October's mid-term elections in Congress.

The International Monetary Fund recommended labor reforms as a way of reducing employment costs and President Carlos Menem tried to push a tough reform package through by decree. Blocked by courts and hostile unions, he tried three-way talks and when they proved fruitless, he made a deal with unions.
Late last month Menem went behind the backs of business leaders to sign a blueprint Act of Agreement with unions, which is a watered-down reform package.

The big business lobby blasts it as "useless" because it maintains union control over wage talks and drops plans to replace costly redundancy payouts with unemployment insurance. It also drops plans to force union-controlled healthcare schemes to compete with private firms in an open market.

Even Economy Minister Roque Fernandez has urged all-out labor reform, rather than these "half-hearted" changes. But unions are bent on sending the Act to Congress in its present form and won the backing of the small business lobby Thursday.
The Labor Minister appears to have sided with the unions too, saying Friday that the "spirit of the Act of Agreement will be maintained" and making this apparent dig at employers:
"It would be very easy for the country to solve the problem of unemployment by cutting wages or erasing collective agreements and the unions."

The CGT source said employers appeared to have accepted by Friday the "union and government proposal that redundancy pay be fixed at 70 percent," but there was little progress on the thorniest issue, which is centralized pay talks.

"On that issue, the CGT is not prepared to change one single letter," said the source, predicting that next week's talks would probably produce two documents, one on agreed points and one on disputed points, for Congress to debate.
